Adding a named `rightComponent?: ReactNode` slot prop (together with its companion `shouldShowRightComponent?: boolean` flag) to `DropdownOption` is the ReactNode-slot-prop configuration anti-pattern. The options are `.map()`'d and spread into `PopoverMenu`/`MenuItem` (`menuItems={options.map((item) => ({...item}))}` in `ButtonWithDropdownMenu/index.tsx`), so every new positional slot widens a config-array-driven surface: the component must know about each slot and consumers cannot compose, reorder, or wrap it. This is exactly the illustrated bad example, which uses `rightComponent?: ReactNode` + `shouldShowRightComponent`.

Prefer composing the toggle row as an explicit child/compound-component slot rather than threading arbitrary JSX through the option config. For example, expose a dedicated menu-row component the consumer renders directly instead of passing `rightComponent`/`shouldShowRightComponent` in the option object:
```tsx
<ButtonWithDropdownMenu.Menu>
    <ButtonWithDropdownMenu.ToggleRow
        title={translate('workspace.categories.showCategoryGLCodes')}
        isOn={policy?.showCategoryGLCodes ?? false}
        onToggle={(value) => setPolicyShowCategoryGLCodes(policyId, value)}
    />
</ButtonWithDropdownMenu.Menu>
```
so adding a new row type never requires expanding `DropdownOption`.

`ConfirmationFieldList` now takes a `renderTransactionDetailsFields: (props: DetailsFieldsProps) => React.ReactNode` render-function prop and calls it inline to fill a fixed slot in its layout. This is configuration via a render prop (Case 5): each variant supplies a `render*` function and `ConfirmationFieldList` owns the slot, so adding a new renderable area means expanding the prop interface rather than adding a composable child. The refactor otherwise moves away from boolean-flag config, so this render prop is the one place the config pattern is reintroduced.

Prefer exposing the details area as a compound-component child (a slot) instead of a `render*` prop, e.g. let the variant pass the details fields as `children` (or a `<ConfirmationFieldList.Details>` slot) and read the computed `fieldVisibility`/`flags` from context, so the list never has to know about each type's details component:

```tsx
<ConfirmationFieldList policy={policy} ...>
    <ConfirmationFieldList.Details>
        <TimeDetailsFields .../>
    </ConfirmationFieldList.Details>
</ConfirmationFieldList>
```

This new `HeaderWithBackButton` reintroduces a monolithic, configuration-heavy prop interface: a long list of `shouldShow*`/`shouldDisplay*` boolean flags (`shouldShowReportAvatarWithDisplay`, `shouldShowBackButton`, `shouldShowCloseButton`, `shouldShowDownloadButton`, `shouldShowThreeDotsButton`, `shouldDisplaySearchRouter`, `shouldDisplayHelpButton`, etc.) plus optional content props (`icon`, `policyAvatar`) that each map 1:1 to a conditional render block inside the body. This is exactly the Case 1 (boolean-flag) + Case 3 (monolithic interface) anti-pattern the rule targets, and per the rule a refactor that creates a new component still following the configuration pattern should be flagged.

I understand from the PR description this is intentional scaffolding to keep the legacy flat API while the composition primitives are built. To align with the composition target, prefer wiring the primitives through composed children (`Header.Left`/`Header.Right` + block children) so consumers add/remove features by including/excluding blocks rather than toggling flags:

```tsx
<Header>
    <Header.Left>
        {shouldShowBackButton && <HeaderBackButton onPress={onBackButtonPress} />}
        {!!icon && <HeaderIcon src={icon} />}
        <HeaderTitle>{title}</HeaderTitle>
    </Header.Left>
    <Header.Right>
        {children}
        {shouldShowThreeDotsButton && <HeaderThreeDotsMenu items={threeDotsMenuItems} />}
    </Header.Right>
</Header>
```

The new `shouldFillAvailableHeight?: boolean` flag is a configuration flag that toggles layout strategy and behavior across the component body: it switches the `NegatableFilter` style (`shouldFillAvailableHeight ? styles.flex1 : undefined`), whether the input is wrapped in `AutoGrowHeightInputContainer` vs rendered directly, `textInputContainerStyles`, `autoGrowHeight`, `submitBehavior`/`onSubmitEditing`, and whether `<Button.KeyboardShortcut />` is shown. Each new fill-height requirement forces another branch inside this component.

Prefer composition over a boolean flag — e.g. expose the fill-height layout as a separate composable variant/wrapper (the callers `TextInputFilterContentPageWrapper` vs `TextInputFilterContentPopupWrapper` already differ) so the compact and fill-height behaviors are distinct building blocks rather than `shouldFillAvailableHeight ? ... : ...` branches threaded through one component.

The new `shouldDisplaySubmitButtonAndFooterInOneRowInLandscapeMode` boolean flag is a layout-strategy configuration prop (Case 1). It is threaded through `FormProvider` -> `FormWrapper` -> `FormAlertWithSubmitButton`, where it drives `shouldDisplayButtonAndFooterInOneRow` and branches the layout inside the component (`styles.flexRow`/`styles.gap3` on the wrapper `View`, `styles.flex1` vs `styles.mb3` on the button, footer placement). Each new landscape layout need would require another flag and more internal branching, coupling every consumer to this component's internals.

Prefer expressing the footer/submit arrangement compositionally. For example, let the consumer control the footer container layout (it already passes `footerContent` and `shouldRenderFooterAboveSubmit`), or expose the submit button and footer as composable children so the one-row-in-landscape arrangement lives at the call site rather than as a boolean threaded through three components.

The new `shouldHideHeader?: boolean` flag is a Case 1 boolean-flag configuration: it drives a ternary inside the component body (`return shouldHideHeader ? <ActivityIndicator .../> : <FullScreenLoadingIndicator .../>`) that selects between two rendering strategies. Per the rule, a prop that toggles which loading UI renders is a behavioral flag, not presentational, and adding it to this widely-used generic HOC couples it to a consumer-specific render context. The PR description itself flags this as an open design question.

Prefer signaling the render context abstractly rather than a header-specific boolean — e.g. let the caller pass the loading component to render (composition), or expose an explicit `LoadingIndicator` slot/prop so `IOURequestStartPage` supplies the `ActivityIndicator` and standalone RHP routes get the fullscreen loader, without the HOC branching on a `shouldHideHeader` flag. This keeps the HOC's contract context-free and avoids expanding its API each time a new render context needs different loading UI.

The new optional `emptyState?: React.ReactNode` prop is a configuration slot: its sole purpose is to conditionally render UI in place of the picker (`{emptyState ?? <SearchSingleSelectionPicker .../>}`). Every time a consumer needs to swap in different content (disabled empty state, loading indicator, etc.) the slot prop and its conditional branch have to be threaded through `RuleSelectionBase`, coupling the component to each consumer's needs. This is the ReactNode-slot anti-pattern (Case 2/3) — favor composition over configuration.

Prefer letting the consumer own the layout via composition instead of a slot prop. For example, expose the picker as a child/compound piece and let the caller decide what to render:

```tsx
<RuleSelectionBase titleKey="common.category" ...>
    {emptyState ?? <RuleSelectionBase.Picker />}
</RuleSelectionBase>
```

This keeps `RuleSelectionBase` stable while callers compose the empty/loading/picker states themselves.

The new `shouldShowCustomDate` boolean prop is a configuration flag whose sole purpose is to conditionally render the "Custom date" `MenuItem` (`{shouldShowCustomDate && (<MenuItem ... />)}`). This is the composition-over-configuration anti-pattern (Case 1/Case 2): a `shouldShow*` flag that toggles element visibility is a behavioral flag, and every new consumer cements the config-driven API. Adding more visibility toggles to this component grows its surface area and coupling over time.

Prefer expressing this as composition so consumers include/omit the element rather than toggling it via a prop. For example, let the caller decide whether the custom-date option is present by composing it in, instead of the component branching on a flag:

```tsx
// Consumer that wants the option composes it in; consumer that doesn't simply omits it.
// The component renders its children/slots and never needs a shouldShowCustomDate branch.
```

If a compositional refactor is out of scope here, at minimum keep this flag from proliferating — the presence/absence of the custom-date option should be driven by composition rather than an ever-growing set of `shouldShow*` booleans.

This adds two new optional content props (`buttonTranslationKey`, `onButtonPress`) to `BlockingView` whose sole purpose is to conditionally render a UI element. Both props are used only inside this `{!!onButtonPress && !!buttonTranslationKey && (<Button .../>)}` block — nothing else. Per Case 2, an optional prop that exists only to gate a `{!!prop && <Element />}` render should be a composable child instead. Every future addition (e.g. a second action, an icon on the button) would again require expanding `BlockingView`'s prop interface and internals, increasing coupling and regression risk.

Prefer composition so `BlockingView` never has to change when a consumer needs a CTA. For example, expose the button as a child the consumer opts into rather than a prop pair:

```tsx
// Consumer (e.g. FullPageErrorView / SpendOverTimeSectionContent) composes the action:
<BlockingView icon={...} title={...} subtitle={...}>
    <BlockingView.Action onPress={retry}>{translate('common.tryAgain')}</BlockingView.Action>
</BlockingView>
```

This keeps `BlockingView` stable and lets each consumer decide whether (and what) to render below the subtitle without threading `buttonTranslationKey`/`onButtonPress` through `FullPageErrorView` as pure pass-throughs.

The new `isCompact` boolean flag adds yet another layout-strategy toggle to `ReceiptEmptyState`, which already carries several branching flags (`isThumbnail`, `isInMoneyRequestView`, `shouldUseFullHeight`, `isDisplayedInWideRHP`). Here it drives an entire `isCompact ? (...) : (...)` ternary that swaps between two complete render trees inside the component. This is configuration-by-flag: every new visual variant requires modifying this component's API and internals rather than composing it from the outside.

Prefer expressing the compact banner as a composable variant/sub-component the consumer opts into, rather than threading another boolean through the component. For example, extract the shared icon markup into a small internal component and let the caller render the compact layout (`<ReceiptEmptyState.CompactBanner .../>`) or a dedicated `CompactReceiptEmptyState` wrapper, keeping `ReceiptEmptyState` stable as variants grow.

The new `minItemsForSearchBar` prop is configuration that gates whether an internal UI element renders: its sole effect is the conditional `{shouldShowSearchBar && <TableSearchBar label={label} />}` block below. `Table` is already a compound/composition component (`Table.FilterBar`, `Table.Header`, `Table.Body`, `Table.NoResultsState`), so search-bar presence should be expressed compositionally (the consumer includes or omits the search bar) rather than by threading a numeric threshold prop that branches inside the component. Each new threshold/flag prop enlarges the component's API and couples every consumer to its internals.

Suggested fix: expose the search bar as a composable child (e.g. `Table.SearchBar`) that the consumer renders or not, and let `DomainGroupsTable` decide whether to include it based on the item count, instead of adding `minItemsForSearchBar` to `TableFilterBar`:

```tsx
// DomainGroupsTable
<Table.FilterBar label={translate('domain.groups.findGroup')}>
    {groups.length >= CONST.DOMAIN_GROUPS_SEARCH_BAR_THRESHOLD && <Table.SearchBar label={translate('domain.groups.findGroup')} />}
</Table.FilterBar>
```

`shouldFillContainer?: boolean` is a behavioral flag (Case 1): it selects between layout strategies inside the component body (`shouldFillContainer ? styles.flex1 : undefined`). Props that toggle a rendering/layout strategy are not purely presentational — they push layout decisions into the component and grow its config surface.

Let the consumer own the outer container instead of toggling it via a flag — e.g. drop the wrapping `View`/flex handling and have the parent (`WorkspaceCompanyCardsBalanceLabels`) apply `flex1` (or not) when it composes each label, keeping `WorkspaceCardLabel` free of layout-strategy configuration.

`renderPopoverContent?: (closePopover: () => void) => ReactNode` is a render-function prop (Case 5). The component fills a slot of its own layout by calling `renderPopoverContent?.(() => setVisible(false))`, and each new renderable popover area would require expanding this interface. Render functions are configuration disguised as flexibility — the component still owns the slot.

Prefer exposing the popover body as a composable child so consumers declare it as JSX rather than a callback the component must invoke. If the child truly needs the close action, expose it via context (e.g. a `WorkspaceCardLabel.PopoverContent` compound sub-component that reads a `closePopover` from context) instead of a `render*` prop.

The `shouldShowAvatar` boolean flag selects between two entirely different rendering strategies inside the component (`if (!shouldShowAvatar) { return <Button icon={...} /> } return <Button>...avatar+text...</Button>`). This is a behavioral flag (Case 1) rather than a presentational one — it toggles which content the button renders. Every future variant would require another flag and another branch, growing the component's API and internals.

Prefer composition: expose the button's inner content via `children`, or split into two small focused components (e.g. `AccountManagerBookCallButton` and `AccountManagerBookCallButtonWithAvatar`) so callers pick the variant by rendering the right one, and the shared `<Button>` wrapper stays stable.

```tsx
// Consumer decides the leading content — no boolean flag
<AccountManagerBookCallButton calendarLink={link}>
    <Icon src={icons.Phone} />
</AccountManagerBookCallButton>

<AccountManagerBookCallButton calendarLink={link}>
    <Avatar avatarID={accountManagerAccountID} .../>
</AccountManagerBookCallButton>
```

The new optional `bulkActionsButton?: React.ReactNode` prop is a positional ReactNode slot whose sole purpose is conditional rendering — it is only consumed as `{bulkActionsButton ?? (<>…</>)}`. This is configuration disguised as flexibility: every new piece of UI the header needs to swap in/out forces another slot prop and another conditional inside this component, increasing its coupling and surface area.

Prefer composition over a slot prop. Let the consumer compose the controls directly (e.g. expose a compound child like `<WorkspaceCompanyCardsTableHeader.Controls>` or pass `children`) so the header doesn't need to know about `bulkActionsButton` at all:

```tsx
// header renders its children/slot without a dedicated prop
<WorkspaceCompanyCardsTableHeader>
    {selectedCards.length > 0 ? <BulkActionsButton /> : <DefaultControls />}
</WorkspaceCompanyCardsTableHeader>
```

This new component takes `SearchTableHeader?: React.JSX.Element` as a named JSX-slot prop (renamed to `searchTableHeader` and only forwarded into `SelectionTopBar`/used in conditionals). A named `ReactElement` slot prop whose only job is to render UI in a specific position is configuration (Case 2), not composition — the parent owns layout and every new slot expands the interface.

Consider passing the header as a composed child rather than a positional slot prop so the table header can evolve without changing `ExpenseFlatSearchView`'s contract.

`SelectionTopBar` is a new component that accepts `SearchTableHeader?: React.JSX.Element` as a named JSX-slot prop whose sole purpose is to be rendered in a fixed position (`{SearchTableHeader}` further down). Per Case 2, a named `ReactNode`/`ReactElement` prop used only to fill a slot is configuration, not composition — the consumer can't reorder or wrap it, and adding a new slot means changing this component's interface.

Prefer composing the header as a child instead of threading it through a slot prop:

```tsx
// SelectionTopBar renders {children} (or a <SelectionTopBar.Header> sub-component)
<SelectionTopBar isLargeScreenWidth={isLargeScreenWidth} canSelectMultiple={canSelectMultiple} /* ...counts... */>
    {searchTableHeader}
</SelectionTopBar>
```

This migrates the consumer from the `subtitle` string prop to the `renderSubtitle` render-function prop. Render-function props are configuration disguised as flexibility — `Section` must own the slot and manage the fallback between `renderSubtitle()` and the default `subtitle`. The rule calls out `renderSubtitle` explicitly as a Case 5 anti-pattern, and each new consumer cements the config-heavy API and makes a future compositional refactor harder. New consumers of config-heavy APIs should be flagged at the same severity as the creator.

Prefer composing the subtitle as a child block rather than passing a render function, e.g.:

```tsx
<Section isCentralPane renderTitle={renderTitle} childrenStyles={[styles.gap3]}>
    <Section.Subtitle>
        <Text style={[styles.textNormal, styles.colorMuted]}>{translate('workspace.rules.agentRules.subtitle')}</Text>
        {!!ruleBotAccountID && (
            <View style={[styles.flexRow, styles.alignItemsCenter, styles.gap2]}>
                <Text style={[styles.textNormal, styles.colorMuted]}>{translate('workspace.rules.agentRules.enforcedBy')}</Text>
                <UserPill accountID={ruleBotAccountID} avatar={ruleBot?.avatar} displayName={ruleBotDisplayName} email={ruleBot?.login} />
            </View>
        )}
    </Section.Subtitle>
    {/* ...rest of section content... */}
</Section>
```

If `Section` does not yet expose subtitle composition, advocate for a compositional sub-component instead of adopting the render-function prop.

This adds a `headerComponent?: ReactElement` slot prop to the shared `Table`, which is rendered inside `TableBody` via `ListHeaderComponent={headerComponent ?? ListHeaderComponent}`. A named `ReactElement` prop whose purpose is to render UI in a specific position is configuration, not composition — and notably this moves the `Table` away from its existing compositional API (``, ``, ``) that the wrappers previously used. Every new slot the consumer needs would require modifying `Table`'s props and internals. Prefer a composable child the consumer includes/omits, so the slot stays a building block rather than a prop the component must know about: ```tsx {pageHeader}
```

The `EmptyStateComponent: React.ReactElement` prop is a named ReactElement slot whose sole purpose is conditional rendering (`{isEmpty && EmptyStateComponent}`). This is configuration rather than composition — the component must know about the empty-state slot, and adding new slots would require expanding the prop interface. The shared `Table` is already a compound component, so the empty state should be expressed as a composable child instead of threading a ReactElement through props. Let the consumer compose the empty state directly as children of `Table` (or a dedicated `Table.EmptyState`/conditional child), removing the `EmptyStateComponent` prop: ```tsx {isEmpty ? emptyStateContent : ( <> {tags.length >= CONST.STANDARD_LIST_ITEM_LIMIT && } )}
``` so `WorkspaceTagsTable` no longer needs to accept a UI element as a prop.

This newly-extracted component is built around a large configuration interface rather than composition. `BaseFeatureTrainingContentProps` threads many boolean flags (`shouldShowDismissModalOption`, `shouldRenderSVG`, `shouldRenderHTMLDescription`, `shouldCloseOnConfirm`, `shouldUseScrollView`, `shouldShowConfirmationLoader`, `canConfirmWhileOffline`) and optional content props (`title`, `description`, `secondaryDescription`, `helpText`) through props, each mapping 1:1 to a conditional render block inside the component body. Adding a new feature requires expanding this prop interface and modifying the component internals. Since this refactor is creating a brand-new component, it's an opportunity to favor composition: expose composable sub-components (e.g., `<FeatureTrainingContent.Illustration>`, `<FeatureTrainingContent.DismissOption>`, `<FeatureTrainingContent.HelpButton>`) so consumers include only the blocks they need and the component never changes when new features are added.

Extract the conditionally-rendered regions into compound sub-components driven by `children` instead of boolean/content configuration props.

The new `EmptyStateComponent: React.ReactElement` prop is a named ReactElement slot whose sole purpose is conditional rendering (`{!hasRules && EmptyStateComponent}`). This is configuration disguised as a slot — adding/removing an empty state forces the table's API and internals to change, and the consumer can't control its placement. Since `Table` is already a compound/composition component (`Table.SearchBar`, `Table.Header`, `Table.Body`), the empty state should be expressed as a composable child rather than a prop. Suggested fix: drop the `EmptyStateComponent` prop and let the consumer render the empty state as a child of `Table` (or a dedicated `Table.EmptyState` block), e.g.: ```tsx {!hasRules && } {hasRules && (<>)}
```

This adds a new consumer of `MenuItemWithTopDescription`'s `furtherDetailsComponent` slot prop — a named `ReactElement` configuration slot. Passing JSX through a named prop is configuration disguised as flexibility: the `MenuItem`/`MenuItemWithTopDescription` component must own a dedicated conditional render block for this slot, and each new consumer cements the config pattern, making future refactoring harder. The consumer also can't control composition or ordering of the slot.

Prefer composition: extract the `PressableWithoutFeedback` Google-search block into its own focused component (e.g., `GoogleMerchantSearchLink`) and render it as explicit sibling JSX next to the merchant menu item, rather than threading JSX through the `furtherDetailsComponent` prop. This keeps the render tree visible in the consumer and avoids expanding the config-driven slot API.

`BaseWidgetItem` is called out in the rule as the canonical example of a configuration-heavy component (Case 2 -- content props whose sole purpose is conditional rendering). Adding a new consumer cements the config pattern and makes future refactoring to a compositional API harder.

Consider using a compound-component API instead:

```tsx
<WidgetItem.Container>
    <WidgetItem.Icon src={ExpensifyCardIcon} backgroundColor={theme.widgetIconBG} fill={theme.widgetIconFill} />
    <WidgetItem.Content>
        <WidgetItem.Subtitle>{translate('homePage.timeSensitiveSection.addVirtualCardPersonalDetails.subtitle')}</WidgetItem.Subtitle>
        <WidgetItem.Title>{translate('homePage.timeSensitiveSection.addVirtualCardPersonalDetails.title')}</WidgetItem.Title>
    </WidgetItem.Content>
    <WidgetItem.Action onPress={() => Navigation.navigate(ROUTES.MISSING_PERSONAL_DETAILS.getRoute(String(card.cardID)))}>
        {translate('homePage.timeSensitiveSection.addVirtualCardPersonalDetails.cta')}
    </WidgetItem.Action>
</WidgetItem.Container>
```

If a compositional `WidgetItem` API does not yet exist, consider creating it or advocating for one -- each new `BaseWidgetItem` consumer increases the cost of that future migration.

Adding a new `actions?: React.ReactNode` slot prop to `Banner` is a Case 2 violation — its sole purpose is to conditionally render custom content in the action area (`{actions ?? (shouldShowButton && ...)}`). Each new ReactNode slot prop cements the configuration pattern and makes future refactoring harder.

Consider a composition-based approach where the consumer controls what renders via children or compound components, e.g.:
```tsx
<Banner text={translate('concierge.enableNotifications.prompt')} ...>
  <Button success small text={translate('concierge.enableNotifications.cta')} onPress={requestAndDismiss} />
  <Button small style={[styles.ml2]} text={translate('common.notNow')} onPress={dismissForSession} />
</Banner>
```
This keeps Banner stable — new action layouts never require changing its prop interface.

This PR adds four new configuration props to `Banner` (`shouldShowSecondaryButton`, `secondaryButtonText`, `onSecondaryButtonPress`, `shouldUseSmallButtons`) that control conditional rendering via boolean flags. The `shouldShowSecondaryButton` prop's sole purpose is to gate `{shouldShowSecondaryButton && !!secondaryButtonText && <Button ... />}` — a Case 2 violation (content prop configuration). Similarly, `shouldUseSmallButtons` is a Case 1 boolean flag that toggles button sizing behavior.

Consider composing the buttons as children instead of configuring them via props. For example, the `EnableNotificationsBanner` consumer could render its own action buttons:
```tsx
<Banner text={translate('concierge.enableNotifications.prompt')}>
    <Button success small text={translate('concierge.enableNotifications.cta')} onPress={requestAndDismiss} />
    <Button small text={translate('common.notNow')} onPress={dismissForSession} style={[styles.ml2]} />
</Banner>
```
This avoids expanding Banner's prop interface for every new button variant.

The `isEditOnly` boolean flag controls whether `<Composer.Footer>` is rendered inside the component. This is a Case 1 violation (boolean flag configuration): the component already uses the composition pattern internally with sub-components (`Composer.Footer`, `Composer.Box`, etc.), but this new prop adds a configuration flag to toggle feature presence from outside.

Instead of a boolean flag, consider one of these approaches:
1. Have the `Composer` detect edit-only mode from existing context (e.g., `useReportActionActiveEdit` + `useResponsiveLayout`) so it can decide internally whether to show the footer, following the "let components own their behavior" principle.
2. If the footer must be controlled externally, use composition: expose a `ComposerEditOnly` variant or let the consumer compose without `<Composer.Footer>` by making the footer an optional child block rather than always-present-but-conditionally-hidden.

A new optional `supportingText` prop is being added to `BaseWidgetItem` whose sole purpose is conditional rendering: `{!!supportingText && <Text style={styles.widgetItemSubtitle}>{supportingText}</Text>}`. This is a Case 2 violation -- adding another optional content prop that maps 1:1 to a conditional render block. The existing `subtitle` prop already follows this same anti-pattern.

Instead of growing `BaseWidgetItem`'s prop interface with each new content element, refactor toward a compound component (composition) pattern where consumers include or omit sub-components as children:

```tsx
<WidgetItem.Container onPress={onCtaPress}>
    <WidgetItem.Icon src={icon} backgroundColor={theme.widgetIconBG} />
    <WidgetItem.Content>
        <WidgetItem.Subtitle>{subtitle}</WidgetItem.Subtitle>
        <WidgetItem.Title>{title}</WidgetItem.Title>
        <WidgetItem.Subtitle>{supportingText}</WidgetItem.Subtitle>
    </WidgetItem.Content>
    <WidgetItem.Action onPress={onCtaPress}>{ctaText}</WidgetItem.Action>
</WidgetItem.Container>
```

This way, adding new content elements never requires modifying `BaseWidgetItem`'s props or internals.

The new `shouldShowFromPrefix` boolean prop is a configuration flag that conditionally renders the "from" `<Text>` element (line 242: `{shouldShowFromPrefix && <Text ...>}`). This is a Case 1 violation: a boolean flag controls feature presence inside the component. The consumer (`ReportDetailsPage`) sets `shouldShowFromPrefix={false}` and then provides its own "from" label externally via `description={translate('threads.from')}` on the wrapping `MenuItemWithTopDescription`, which confirms the prefix is a composable concern rather than an internal toggle.

Instead of adding a boolean flag, consider composing the "from" prefix outside the component. For example, the consumer could render the prefix text alongside `ParentNavigationSubtitle` directly:

```tsx
// In ReportDetailsPage - compose the prefix externally
<View style={styles.flexRow}>
    <Text style={[styles.optionAlternateText, styles.textLabelSupporting]}>
        {translate('threads.from')}
    </Text>
    <ParentNavigationSubtitle ... />
</View>
```

This avoids adding a boolean toggle to the component's API and lets consumers decide whether to show the prefix through composition.

The new `secondaryAction` optional prop is a Case 2 violation (content prop configuration). Its sole purpose is to conditionally render a `<Button>` via `{!!secondaryAction && (<Button .../>)}`. This adds a configuration-driven slot to the component.

Consider accepting `children` or a composable child pattern instead, so callers can pass additional action buttons directly:
```tsx
<FrozenCardHeader ...>
    <Button text={translate('workspace.common.viewTransactions')} icon={expensifyIcons.MoneySearch} onPress={navigateToTransactions} />
</FrozenCardHeader>
```

Same Case 4 violation: the `actionButtons` array is a static config array of known items (update card, view transactions) mapped through `CardDetailsActionButtons`. Declare each button as explicit JSX instead of encoding them as a data array.

Same Case 4 violation as `ExpensifyCardPage`: the `actionButtons` array is a static config array of known items (freeze, view transactions) with conditional entries, mapped through `CardDetailsActionButtons`. Declare each button as explicit JSX instead of encoding them as a data array.

The `actionButtons` array is a static config array of statically-known items (freeze card, view transactions) with conditional entries via spread, mapped through the generic `CardDetailsActionButtons` component. This is Case 4 (config-array driven rendering). Business logic (conditional freeze button) is mixed into the data declaration.

Instead, render each action as explicit declarative JSX, using a shared layout wrapper that accepts `children` for consistent styling:
```tsx
<CardActionButtonsRow>
    {canManageCardFreeze && !isCardFrozen(currentCard) && (
        <Button text={translate('cardPage.freezeCard')} icon={expensifyIcons.FreezeCard} onPress={handleFreezePress} isDisabled={isOffline} />
    )}
    <Button text={translate('workspace.common.viewTransactions')} icon={expensifyIcons.MoneySearch} onPress={navigateToTransactions} />
</CardActionButtonsRow>
```

The `shouldOpenParticipantPicker` boolean flag is a configuration prop that drives internal behavior via a `useEffect` (syncing the prop into `isParticipantPickerVisible` state). This couples the parent's decision logic ("should the picker be open?") to the child's internal state management through a boolean flag.

Instead of passing a boolean flag that the child mirrors into state, consider either:
1. Lifting the `isParticipantPickerVisible` state to the parent and passing it directly along with a setter, or
2. Exposing an imperative handle (`ref.openParticipantPicker()`) for the parent to call, or
3. Having the parent render the `ParticipantPicker` itself (composition) rather than telling the child to do so via a flag.

Option 3 (composition) is the most aligned with this rule: the parent decides whether a picker is needed and renders it alongside `MoneyRequestConfirmationList`, rather than configuring the list to internally manage a picker.

`CameraViewport` has 17 props, forming a monolithic configuration interface (Case 3). The flash button sub-feature (`canUseMultiScan`, `flash`, `hasFlash`, `setFlash`, `boltIcon`) is conditionally rendered inside this component and could be extracted into its own `FlashButton` component that owns its icon loading and state display. The camera viewfinder portion (camera ref, device, format, fps, gesture, animated styles) could also be a separate composable block. This would reduce the prop count and allow each piece to evolve independently.

`ScannerControlsBar` has 19 props, making it a monolithic configuration consumer (Case 3). Beyond the icon props that could be loaded internally (see CLEAN-REACT-PATTERNS-2), the component mixes state setters (`setFlash`, `setIsAttachmentPickerActive`, `setIsLoaderVisible`), behavioral flags (`isMultiScanEnabled`, `canUseMultiScan`, `shouldAcceptMultipleFiles`), and domain state (`cameraPermissionStatus`, `flash`, `hasFlash`).
